cues.text: Born in October 1480 at Vicenza, Cajetan earned a doctorate in both civil and canon law at Padua by twenty-four.
By 1506, he had become a prothonotary apostolic at Pope Julius II’s court in Rome, where he played a notable role reconciling the Republic of Venice with the papacy during political tension.
From Court to the Oratory of Divine Love
After Julius II's death, Cajetan withdrew from papal court life.

Though not yet ordained, he is credited with founding the Oratory of Divine Love , an association of pious priests and prelates dedicated to personal sanctification and charitable works that soon spread to other Italian cities.
Ordained a priest only in 1516, he returned to Vicenza the following year and founded a hospital for incurables there, an early expression of the active charity that would mark his entire life.

Returning to Rome in 1523, Cajetan laid the groundwork for a new religious congregation of priests combining monastic discipline with active pastoral ministry, canonically established by Pope Clement VII in 1524.
Among his co-founders was Giovanni Pietro Caraffa , Bishop of Chieti (in Latin, Theate) — later Pope Paul IV — whose title gave the new community its popular name: the Theatines .

The small Theatine community, then numbering only twelve, endured brutal treatment during the catastrophic Sack of Rome in 1527, escaping to Venice, where Cajetan met and assisted St. Jerome Emiliani in establishing his own new congregation devoted to orphan care.
In 1533, Cajetan founded a Theatine house in Naples, where his preaching and example helped check the early spread of Lutheran ideas into Italy.
In Naples, Cajetan confronted the widespread practice of usury directly by founding a charitable pawnshop, a monte di pietà .

It offered the poor loans without exploitative interest and grew over time into what became the Bank of Naples, a lasting practical legacy of his concern for the economically vulnerable alongside his spiritual reforms.

Cajetan died at Naples in 1547 and was canonized in 1671 by Pope Clement X. Though the Theatines never grew into a large order, their vow against begging alms restricted membership to those with independent means.

Cajetan's model combined rigorous personal holiness with active reforming engagement in the Church's public life, placing him among the most influential figures preparing the ground for the broader Catholic Reformation that followed at the Council of Trent .
